boundary: the release itself: every spatial or temporal memory defect live in the ported 5.36.3, whatever allocator holds the memory
title: Eleven spatial and temporal defects live in Perl 5.36.3, each measured live at the pin and clean at master, with what each arm sees
live_in_pin_note: Liveness is measured in both directions for every case, not inferred: each trigger reports under ASan on a build of the pin's own tree and is silent on the same trigger, same harness and same ASan options on master. The dates alone would not settle it -- four of the eleven fixes are DATED BEFORE the v5.36.3 tag (2023-11-28) and are still absent from it, because they landed on blead and were never backported to the 5.36 maintenance branch. Each case therefore records the ancestry that was actually checked with git merge-base --is-ancestor, in both directions.
note: The population was every commit from v5.36.3 to the master tip that touches both C source and a test (457 of 9537), filtered to the ones whose diff has the shape of a spatial or temporal memory defect and triaged by hand against the pin's sources. All eleven cases here are in scope by construction: this corpus admits only spatial and temporal memory defects, which is the study's scope, so unlike the mruby corpus it carries no null dereferences, type confusions or stack-exhaustion rows. Two of the eleven are outside every arm's denominator and say so in their own files: 254b30e378 carries harness_limit because its in-memory filehandle discards its writes in a domain, so the defect never executes, and 9e298ab597's trigger passes its own assertion there. Scoring the arms over all eleven would count those two as misses; the honest denominator is 9. sysalloc-bounds is the baseline: per-object heap bounds are what applications get by default since PR #170, so a catch is a case the bounds arm does not fault on. The nested-allocator arm is sublet-svheads, and it protects ONE of Perl's nested allocators -- the SV head arena. The SV bodies, hash entries and OP slabs keep their upstream allocators, so a case whose stale pointer lives in those is out of that arm's reach by construction and its arm entry says so. All five arms are measured. cheribsd-revocation runs on the CheriBSD image whose loader accepts this binary, with revocation selected per process because the system-wide default kills the guest's own sshd, and every case run under both settings so the pair controls the knob. It reports on 7 of the 11 -- the same count as sublet-svheads but NOT the same 7: they agree on 6, and each catches exactly one the other misses. sublet-svheads alone catches 17535c984a, whose SV head never returns to malloc and so is invisible to any allocator-boundary scheme; cheribsd-revocation alone catches 254b30e378, which the Capstone arms miss only because the domain's in-memory PerlIO layer never executes the defect.
